item.title: GhostAction Attackers Plant Credential Stealer Disguised as Font in 94 GitHub Repositories (2026)
item.description:
The threat actor behind the GhostAction supply chain attack has expanded beyond injecting malicious GitHub Actions workflows into compromised projects to phish open-source developers and deliver a stealer malware disguised within a fake font file.

The latest evolution, detailed by OpenSourceMalware, signals that the attackers are actively refining their modus operandi in response to steps taken by GitHub to prevent the workflow from running.

According to the threat intelligence platform, the threat actor registered the domain "my-github[.]com" and pointed it at "193.32.204[.]199," the same IP address that's used as an exfiltration endpoint for data harvested from running the malicious workflow.

The domain was registered on October 9, 2026, 17 days after "my-gitlab[.]com" was registered. There is no evidence at this stage to suggest that the two code-hosting-themed domains are operated by the same threat actor.

"It follows the same my-<code-host>.com naming pattern, making it a useful pivot, but current infrastructure does not directly connect it to GhostAction," security researcher Paul McCarty said. "They use different registrars, registrant records, Cloudflare nameserver pairs, IP addresses, ASNs, and DNS designs, and no shared certificate or account artifact has been recovered."

Since then, the "my-github[.]com" domain has been used in a phishing email impersonating a GitHub security alert to target an open-source maintainer. The message, sent from "noreply@my-github[.]com" and on the same day the domain was registered, warned of a suspicious new login to their GitHub account from Moscow, Russia, and instructed them to click on a link to secure their account.

The deceptive page, per OpenSourceMalware, is said to have acted as a reverse proxy, harvesting the victim's password and two-factor authentication (2FA) code, and injected JavaScript that authorized an OAuth app with permissions to modify their workflows so as to facilitate a GhostAction-style attack.

The fake login page also includes JavaScript to silently authorize a GitHub OAuth device flow with repo, workflow, and read:org scopes, granting it broad permissions to read/write repositories, modify Actions workflow files, and gain visibility into organization membership and related organizational data.

The idea is the same as device code phishing, where the end goal is to obtain an access token from GitHub and exfiltrate it to "my-github[.]com" on TCP/8443.

"The script receives a device code and user code, loads /login/device, extracts GitHub's forms from the returned HTML, and submits them automatically," McCarty explained. "It inserts the user code, locates an authorization form, adds authorize=1, and posts the approval through the victim's authenticated proxied session."

"The victim does not need to type the device code or consciously approve the OAuth application. This kit goes further by automating the user-code and authorization steps through the reverse-proxied session."

By stealing a repository-scoped OAuth token, it gives the attacker a reusable API credential. Furthermore, the permissions granted through the stealthy OAuth authorization are consistent with GhostAction's ability to enumerate repositories and inject malicious workflow files under ".github/workflows/."

"The actor can now combine repository-scale automation with individual social engineering against people whose accounts provide access to projects, organizations, registries, and downstream users," OpenSourceMalware said.

To make matters worse, the campaign has also been observed incorporating a second-stage component that persists on developer machines even after the malicious workflow has been removed.

Specifically, the approach takes a leaf out of North Korea's playbook by committing three different files -

  • A Microsoft Visual Studio Code (VS Code) tasks.json file with a "runOn: folderOpen" trigger that causes it to run automatically when the folder is opened in the application.
  • A "public/fonts/fa-solid-400.woff2" file that contains a stealer payload designed to harvest AWS keys, PyPI tokens, npm tokens, Git logins, Kubernetes cluster credentials, SSH private keys, and AI provider credentials for Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini. The font file name is the same as one used in North Korea's Fake Font/PolinRider campaign from January 2026.
  • A second GitHub Actions workflow that's activated if the infostealer never runs.

The VS Code task is set up to auto-run the credential stealer, which, besides collecting data, installs a cron job that runs attacker-supplied code every five minutes. The collected data is sent to the same server over plain HTTP on port 8080. A total of 94 compromised repositories with the second-stage component have been identified.

As for the second CI workflow, it's the same as the original malicious workflow, but with added credential formats to look for and a fallback that uploads findings to a secret GitHub gist if the POST fails. The second workflow goes by the following names -

  • lint.yml
  • ci-check.yml
  • build-check.yml
  • repo-health.yml
  • audit.yml
  • code-review.yml
  • test-suite.yml
  • cache-cleanup.yml

OpenSourceMalware said the 94 repositories belong to 66 owners, out of which 15 have since been deleted, renamed, or made private. Of the still accessible repositories, most of them appear to have been largely abandoned, with one of them left untouched for more than nine years. Sixty-five of the 79 repositories went without a commit for more than a year.

"Stage 1 needs GitHub to run the workflow," OpenSourceMalware said. "On October 9, GitHub started preventing the malicious workflow from running, and the waves on October 10 and 12 extracted no secrets. Stage 2 adds a launcher that doesn't need a runner at all, and it arrived six days after the block. We can’t say the block caused it. We can say the operator moved to a place GitHub's controls don't reach."

To mitigate the threat, developers should revoke GitHub access and tokens from a clean device, change their passwords, audit their repositories, rotate every credential the workflows can reach, and alert users who have cloned the repositories.

"We don't know who the operator is, but their work suggests limited experience," Jenn Gile, co-founder of OpenSourceMalware, told The Hacker News. "The stealer's environment-variable filter misses most API keys, its home-directory search can time out and discard its own results, and a single IP handles exfiltration, phishing, and noisy internet scanning. That last mistake is why searching for the IP still finds infections."

item.title: ⚡ Weekly Recap: 98 Zero-Days, Rogue AI Agents, $100M Crypto Theft, 700 Supermarkets Hit and More (2026)
item.description:
The worst problems don't always come with a warning. Sometimes they arrive through a service everyone trusts, a device someone bought, or a system nobody thought to check. By the time something looks wrong, the damage may already be done.

This week had plenty of that. Trusted connections became a problem. Hardware wasn't as safe as it looked. Old bugs found new victims, and some systems were left so exposed that breaking in barely required any effort. Even AI agents crossed lines they weren't supposed to.

Some attacks were clever. Others were painfully simple. The full recap shows just how much can go wrong, and how little it sometimes takes.

⚡ Threat of the Week

ConnectWise Suspends Cloud Backup Following Unauthorized Access — ConnectWise disabled seven ConnectWise application identities as it continues its investigation into an incident in which unknown threat actors obtained unauthorized access to the application identities and compromised Microsoft 365 tenants. The IT management software provider said it took the action on October 17, 2026, at 07:00 UTC, adding it has also suspended Cloud Backup service by revoking certificates used for affected application connections across all users.

New Priorities for Critical Infrastructure: A Nation-State Threat Roundtable

Replace legacy DB tools with a modern platform that connects to every major database from one interface and eliminates locally stored credentials. Available for download as a free desktop app or as part of KeeperPAM.

 Learn More ➝

🔔 Top News

  • BeyondTrust Remote Support Flaw Exploited as 0-Day — The China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (previously UNC5221 or Warp Panda) exploited a newly disclosed security flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) as a zero-day in late August 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102764 (CVSS score: 9.3), is a case of improper origin validation in an internal messaging component that could be exploited by a remote attacker to perform file operations on an affected appliance. According to Google-owned Mandiant, the attack involved the deployment of a lightweight PHP web shell codenamed SAWFLY for interactive remote access and a tunneling program called BARECLAW to route traffic through the device. Only a small number of organizations are assessed to be impacted.
  • Microsoft Disrupts 3 Phishing Kits Linked to Over 1 Billion Scam Messages — Microsoft says it has dismantled a criminal marketplace that sold three phishing kits, namely CoGUI (aka NX or FA), Haozi (aka Phoenix), and Iron Man System, that were responsible for sending over 1 billion malicious messages to more than 75,000 organizations worldwide. Redmond said it took down Yam Store (aka Storm-3119), a coordinated underground network that offered commercial phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) toolkits that allowed other threat actors to readily purchase and deploy phishing pages and steal data and credentials. The kits were also capable of advanced evasion, such as geofencing, fake CAPTCHA gates, IP address blocklists and allowlists, and anti-detection configurations. Yam Store functioned as an initial access broker, peddling not just phishing kits but also infrastructure built on compromised or fraudulently obtained Microsoft and Google cloud environments.
  • Ledger Finds Unauthorized Hardware Implants — Cryptocurrency hardware maker Ledger temporarily paused sales of its products via CryptoBilis and other third-party resellers in Southeast Asia and Germany after a backdoor embedded into a handful of wallets led to the theft of an estimated $100 million in cryptocurrency. The implants are said to be an advanced version of a backdoor that hardware hacker Joe Grand found earlier this year and notified Ledger in March 2026. It's not clear how this occurred, but signs point to a compromise of Ledger's supply chain. One of the victims of the incident is a fraudster who engaged in a task scam and lost more than $4.8 million. "In this task scam, people were paid to fake sales and reviews of real items," Chainalysis said. "Then a 'negative balance' appeared, and they were told to add their own money in order to get paid. On Sep 22, the person behind the scam moved the proceeds into three separate Ledger addresses. On Oct 9, thieves emptied all three. One transfer each, into the same wallet." According to cybersecurity journalist Kim Zetter, Trezor wallet devices sold by third-party non-authorized sellers have also been found to contain implants that generated pre-determined seed phrases so as to allow the attackers to guess them easily and gain access to the accounts.
  • Pwn2Own Ireland Demos 98 0-Days — The Pwn2Own Ireland 2026 hacking contest saw white-hat hackers exploiting 98 zero-day flaws, earning them a collective $1,262,000 in rewards. Ikotas Labs came first with 42.5 Master of Pwn points and $361,000 in cash after discovering 12 unique bugs. Xint and Team ZyGoat secured second and third spots. Ikotas Labs, Xint, and Mobile Hacking Lab broke into Google's Pixel 10, earning them $150,000, $300,000, and $112,500, respectively. Vendors are expected to patch the zero-days disclosed during the competition within 90 days before the details are publicly disclosed.
  • OpenAI Disclosed New Misalignment Cases — OpenAI said internal models hacked more websites, bypassed browsing restrictions, and used cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn't otherwise access, in the latest set of disclosures where its agents carried out unethical and likely illegal acts. In all, the company reported seven new incidents. The development came as the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it received "multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers" whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, accessed personal data from Indian organizations. The agents found their way in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles. CERT-In did not name the providers or affected organizations.
  • OpenAI Engineer Charged — The U.S. Department of Justice charged an OpenAI engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, with attempting to intercept oral communications after allegedly planting a recording device in an executive conference room. Prosecutors claimed company security staff found a second device in his bag. CCTV footage placed the defendant near the conference room on several dates. Alfozan allegedly had no authority to access or participate in meetings held in the room, which is often reserved for the highest-level discussions. In a subsequent filing, federal prosecutors revealed that Alfozan had booked a one-way ticket from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia with his wife and a third family member before his arrest on October 9, 2026.
  • Attacks on French Refrigeration Systems — Cyber attacks on Danfoss- and Copeland-managed refrigeration systems pushed temperatures as high as 50°C (122°F) for roughly six hours, impacting over 700 French supermarkets and forcing them to discard food. French cybersecurity authorities advised supermarkets to disconnect them from the internet. The attacks targeted Intermarché and Netto, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Monoprix, and E.Leclerc. The affected systems are said to be internet-facing and running outdated firmware. "The username is admin and the password changes every day automatically to.. the current date," security researcher Kevin Beaumont said. "Every single one is like this. You can just log in and change the temperature. Anybody can do it, easily scriptable." To make matters worse, the affected stores likely also failed to put the devices behind a VPN and create an allowlist of trusted IP addresses permitted to log in. "Two things would have changed the outcome," Pen Test Partners said. "Cyber hygiene would have prevented the access: take the controller off the public internet, put remote access behind a VPN and an IP allowlist, bring third-party kit onto the network in a controlled, owned and documented way rather than leaving it on a contractor's own connection, change known and default credentials, and patch to a current release." Multiple vulnerabilities have been disclosed in the affected models, with Claroty warning that the issues could be exploited to "defrost the food."
  • Collabora RCE Flaw Exploited to Backdoor Nextcloud Servers — Threat actors are exploiting a critical command execution flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-110447 (CVSS score: 9.2), in the Collabora Online - Built-in CODE Server app for Nextcloud to backdoor servers. It has been patched in version 26.4.303. The attacks involve issuing a malicious request to the app's "proxy.php" endpoint to trigger command injection and plant a PHP web shell with the end goal of conducting reconnaissance and searching for password databases, password manager artifacts, and cryptocurrency wallets.

This week had plenty of that. Trusted connections became a problem. Hardware wasn't as safe as it looked. Old bugs found new victims, and some systems were left so exposed that breaking in barely required any effort. Even AI agents crossed lines they weren't supposed to.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-102764 (CVSS score: 9.3), is a case of improper origin validation in an internal messaging component that could be exploited by a remote attacker to perform file operations on an affected appliance. According to Google-owned Mandiant, the attack involved the deployment of a lightweight PHP web shell codenamed SAWFLY for interactive remote access and a tunneling program called BARECLAW to route traffic through the device. Only a small number of organizations are assessed to be impacted.

item.title: Popular WordPress SEO Plugin Rank Math PRO Hijacked to Deliver Self-Restoring Backdoor (2026)
item.description:
Copies of Rank Math PRO, the paid version of the Rank Math SEO plugin for WordPress, that were downloaded from rankmath.com or delivered as updates between 20:02 UTC on October 15 and 07:12 UTC on October 16 contained malware, Rank Math said in a security notice published on October 16.

Any site that installed and activated one of those copies should be treated as compromised, and the malware can recreate its hidden backdoor whenever someone visits the site.

Rank Math has removed the affected files and released a clean version, 3.0.124. Installing it replaces the plugin but does not remove files, administrator accounts, or scheduled tasks the malware may already have placed elsewhere on the server, Wordfence said in an advisory on October 17.

Who Is Affected

The version number does not show whether a copy is affected. Rank Math's changelog dates 3.0.123 to October 7, more than a week before the window opened, and the notice limits the incident to copies downloaded or installed through an update during the window.

A copy of 3.0.123 obtained before 20:02 UTC on October 15 is outside it.

The notice sorts sites into three cases:

  • You installed and activated 3.0.123 during the window: treat the site as compromised, even if it has since been updated to 3.0.124, and follow the recovery steps below.
  • You installed it but never activated it: delete the plugin files, install 3.0.124 from your Rank Math account, and run a security scan.
  • You downloaded it but never installed or activated it: nothing in this incident alone indicates the site was compromised.

Rank Math has emailed some users about the incident and told anyone unsure whether the files were installed or activated to contact its support team.

The notice applies only to the PRO plugin, which customers download and update from rankmath.com rather than WordPress.org. The free Rank Math SEO plugin on WordPress.org, which lists more than 4 million active installations and was last updated on October 6, is not named in it.

What the Malware Does

What is known about the malware comes from Rank Math's notice. Neither it nor Wordfence's advisory includes an analysis of the code, and neither names who is behind it.

Deleting suspicious files before stopping what recreates the backdoor may not resolve the problem, which is why the cleanup order below matters. The attacker may also have left PHP backdoor files in other plugins' folders, in theme folders, and in the must-use plugins directory, created administrator accounts, added a fake WordPress core file, changed .htaccess so that .cache files run as PHP, and added scheduled tasks and SSH keys.

Any password, database credential, API key, or other secret the site could reach may have been exposed, and owners should assume it was.

Wordfence assigned the incident CVE-2026-111862 and rates it 9.8 out of 10, with the researcher listed as unknown.

Patchstack classifies it as a backdoor and says that, because the attack was on Rank Math's own systems, "a rule is not possible for mitigation."

How to Recover

Rank Math's preferred recovery is a restore. Where a backup of the site and its database from before 20:02 UTC on October 15 exists, restore it, run a security scan, change every password and credential, and only then install 3.0.124 from your Rank Math account.

Where no clean backup exists, the manual cleanup runs in a fixed order, and three actions come before anything else is touched:

  1. Delete the entire rank-math-pro plugin folder using the hosting file manager or FTP. "Deactivating the plugin alone is not sufficient," the notice says.
  2. In the wp_options table, delete any entry whose option_name is _uf6qdn2hmm, t8krdk990phb or _np5pvf754c.
  3. Block outgoing connections to rank1cdn[.]com if the hosting provider or firewall allows it.

Only then does the search for other changes begin, in these places:

  • Files: PHP files in wp-content/mu-plugins/, in other plugins' folders, in the inc/, includes/ and lib/ folders of non-default themes, in Rank Math's own includes/ folder, and in uploads/.
  • Code: PHP that uses base64_decode with XOR loops, the key xmmqhn, proc_open, or PHP-FPM socket code.
  • File: wp-includes/class-wp-cache-util.php, which is not a WordPress core file.
  • Accounts: administrator usernames beginning wpsupport_, or accounts with email addresses ending @wp-mail[.]net.
  • Server: .htaccess rules that let .cache files run as PHP, .cache files containing PHP code, entries tagged #ms6v46 in the web server user's crontab, WordPress scheduled events, SSH authorized_keys files, other users' crontabs, running processes, and any location outside the site where the web server can write.

Wordfence adds a caution: "Their absence does not, by itself, prove that a website is clean."

item.title: Hackers Exploit Plex2Shell Flaws to Install Crypto Miners and Linux Proxy Backdoor (2026)
item.description:
Threat actors have begun to exploit a chain of vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server to deploy cryptocurrency miners and reverse proxy software, a day after a proof-of-concept (PoC) went public.

According to a researcher who goes by the online alias boredhackerblog, the exploitation activity involves chaining four different vulnerabilities, collectively called Plex2Shell.

The vulnerabilities are below -

  • CVE-2026-96652 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An unauthenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF) stemming via the "/player/timeline" endpoint by taking advantage of the fact that the "protocol" parameter is inserted into a programmatically-constructed player URL with no validation, allowing an attacker to force the Plex server to POST to a destination of their choice.
  • CVE-2026-96654 (CVSS score: 6.9) - An improper neutralization of URL values included in the "searchOne" endpoint that could allow an attacker to call other plugins' functions and supply their own parameters to obtain the owner's admin token.
  • CVE-2026-96655 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An SSRF vulnerability that allows an authenticated user (i.e., the owner token) to request arbitrary internal or external addresses (e.g., an attacker-hosted carrier video carrying the malicious ELF payload) via the '/video/:/transcode/universal' path parameter.
  • CVE-2026-96656 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An external control of file name or path vulnerability that writes the ELF shared object to an attacker-chosen path in the Codecs directory and execute it.

Put differently, the vulnerabilities can be combined together in this order to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on susceptible Plex Media Server instances.

The vulnerabilities, along with CVE-2026-96651 (CVSS score: 7.1), were disclosed to Plex on July 27, 2026, by security researcher Zach Main, and were patched in Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 released on August 3, 2026.

In-the-wild exploitation attempts targeting the flaws have since been recorded a day after technical details of the Plex2Shell chain went public on October 16, 2026. The attacks make use of a shell script to retrieve and deploy a miner payload ("x12345") hosted on a remote server ("217.60.194[.]116") using wget or curl.

The attack efforts have been observed from the following IP addresses -

  • 91.92.40[.]202
  • 176.65.139[.]228
  • 45.194.92[.]222
  • 176.65.139[.]228
The Plex2Shell chain | Source: Zach Main

Furthermore, the vulnerabilities have been exploited to deliver an artifact named "myawesomeproxy," which, according to VirusTotal, is a stealthy Linux backdoor and reverse proxy. Running the program displays the below message, per boredhackerblog -

Running this software on any of your devices makes you agree to the potential external use of your internet traffic.

Also deployed concurrently is an XMRig miner process identified as "mylovelyminer" with its mining server pointing to "ota.proxystream[.]st." Notably, another subdomain associated with the same domain, "global.relay.proxystream[.]st," was flagged by Bitsight in August 2026 in connection with the AISURU DDoS and proxyware botnet.

Posts on Reddit indicate that multiple Plex users have had their instances compromised with the same "mylovelyminer" payload. That said, it's not known at this stage if it stems from the exploitation of Plex2Shell flaws.

The development comes more than a month after Plex urged users to update their instances to the latest version following the release of an update that addressed multiple unspecified security flaws.

It's unclear if the aforementioned vulnerabilities were part of this alert. The Hacker News has contacted Plex for comment and we will update the story if we hear back. In light of active exploitation, users are advised to keep their Plex installations up-to-date for optimal protection.

item.title: Hackers Use New ROMULUS ClickFix Platform to Deliver LegionLoader and Other Malware (2026)
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a ClickFix delivery platform called ROMULUS that's being used to distribute malware such as Legion Loader.

According to Forescout Research - Vedere Labs, ROMULUS is akin to a malware delivery service that employs ClickFix-style lures on bogus landing pages to trick unsuspecting users into running malicious commands and infecting their own machines.

"ROMULUS may be a privately operated panel, a commercial cybercriminal delivery service, an affiliate framework, or software that has been copied between operators," security researcher Sai Molige said in an analysis.

The cybersecurity company said it identified six IP addresses running ROMULUS -

  • 96.62.224[.]81
  • 86.109.75[.]7
  • 151.240.151[.]223
  • 23.94.145[.]224
  • 93.152.224[.]118
  • 2.27.248[.]127

Notably, the IP address "96.62.224[.]81" was identified as hosting a ClickFix script and an MSI installer file in connection with another campaign that has been found to leverage malicious ChatGPT Custom GPTs to direct victims to a fake URL responsible for serving the ClickFix lure.

Forescout's own analysis has since uncovered the same malware being delivered via another server, 86.109.75[.]7, that also hosted a panel codenamed ROMULUS. In addition, a separate chain triggered via ClickFix has been used to run a PowerShell script, which then delivers Legion Loader, a malware loader also called Satacom downloader, CurlyGate, and RobotDropper.

As of writing, it's not known who is behind the ROMULUS platform. However, it shares no overlaps with RomulusLoader, a malware family associated with Silver Fox (aka TA4922), a China-aligned threat actor known for repeatedly using tax-related pretexts to distribute remote access trojans like ValleyRAT (aka Winos 4.0), DcRAT, and potentially Venom RAT via DLL sideloading techniques.

The ROMULUS platform exposes two endpoints that are designed to download a PowerShell staging script, which decides the payload to be fetched next: a trojanized MSI installer carrying a malware loader or an encrypted archive containing Legion Loader that's inflated to nearly 1 GB with repetitive padding to bypass upload limits, sandbox budgets, or static-analysis thresholds. The loader, for its part, communicates with a remote server to fetch and run additional payloads.

The findings indicate how ClickFix is evolving beyond a social engineering technique into a highly effective entry point for malware. To mitigate the threat, it's essential to hunt for suspicious PowerShell commands and DLL sideloading events.

item.title: Ex-OpenAI Engineer Detained in Spy Device Case as Saudi Royal Contacts Emerge (2026)
item.description:
A U.S. court on Monday granted the U.S. government's request to detain a former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a recording device in an executive conference room at the company's San Francisco office to allegedly steal sensitive secrets.

In a new court filing Sunday, prosecutors revealed that Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, was "in frequent communications via WhatsApp with a member of the Saudi Royal Family" throughout 2025 and 2026. Alfozan is said to have communicated with the Saudi royal as recently as October 5, 2026, four days before he was arrested.

"Among other things, the individual told the defendant that an artificial intelligence initiative was being launched in Saudi Arabia and wanted the defendant to join it," the filing reads. "In May 2026, the individual told the defendant, 'Saudi needs you more then [sic] the US!' to which the defendant responded '100,' indicating he agreed."

The Saudi Royal Family member is said to have repeatedly attempted to recruit Alfozan and even asked when he planned to leave OpenAI, to which the defendant said he wouldn't do so until his stock vested.

Alfozan joined OpenAI as an engineer around July 2025 with an annual base salary of $385,000. Last week, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) revealed that he had been arrested for allegedly inserting a stealthy audio recording device into a USB port on the back of a television in the executive conference room to capture sensitive conversations.

The defendant is also said to have modified the device to prevent data transfer between it and the television and encrypted the content stored on the device's microSD card. In addition, he used his wife's personal ChatGPT account to research how to "build a continuous audio recorder" to "captur[e] microphone audio and save compressed WAV recordings to an SD card."

"In the days and weeks before placing the device, the defendant (i) used an OpenAI productivity agent to ascertain which 'meeting rooms' OpenAI 'leadership and exec[utives]' used, and where they met with 'external partners'; and (ii) spent considerable time near the conference room where he later installed the device," the filing said.

Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison.

Prosecutors also argued that Alfozan is a flight risk, stating he has "ample resources... and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government that has (i) no extradition treaty with the United States; (ii) limitless resources; and (iii) the ability to provide extraordinary travel assistance," according to the filing.

Shortly after details of his arrest became public knowledge, it emerged that the defendant had planned to depart to Riyadh with his wife and son on a one-way ticket on October 12, 2026. Although he was arrested three days prior, his wife and son are said to have already left the U.S. without him.

The day before her departure, Alfozan's wife allegedly told the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) agents that her U.S. visa was expiring and that she, along with her son, were permanently shifting back to Saudi Arabia.

"The defendant went to significant lengths to create customized, encrypted recording devices to secretly record highly sensitive meetings involving senior OpenAI personnel and executives, high-level business counterparts, and government officials, all while communicating with individuals of significance in Saudi Arabia and pursuing opportunities in – and making plans to travel to – Saudi Arabia," the filing said.

Stating the U.S. government's investigation is ongoing, prosecutors said a search of the defendant's residence and a "preliminary review" of his electronic devices, including his cellphone, uncovered several pieces of evidence -

  • Several electronic components similar to those in the customized devices the defendant installed in the OpenAI conference room and had in his missing bag were identified in his residence.
  • Photographs from his iPhone dated between September 22 and 28, 2026, that depict one additional concealed recording device, as well as what appear to be the input/output panels on TVs and other electronic devices in various locations in OpenAI buildings, including a second conference room where sensitive meetings took place.
  • A deleted note on his cellphone from September 2026 included links to various recording devices, including those made by Seeed Studio, the same manufacturer whose devices were found in OpenAI's offices and his residence.
  • Browsing history showed that the defendant accessed a folder called "Saudi Gov Docs" on October 4, 2026, and he used an OpenAI productivity agent to inquire about various Saudi-related business and government-related engagements from the Saudi Ministry of Communication and Information Technology (MCIT) between July 6, 2026, and September 21, 2026.

"The defendant leveraged his skills as a highly-educated engineer to create sophisticated recording devices that – the evidence strongly suggests – he intended to bring with him to Saudi Arabia," the filing said.

"Whether the defendant wanted to record OpenAI meetings to enrich himself by enhancing his own business prospects, or to provide aid a foreign government, or both, his conduct is criminal and it presents a danger to innovation in the Silicon Valley and a concern for the national security of the United States."

item.title: ClickFix Attackers Exploit Siemens Software Center Flaw to Deploy Remote Access Trojan (2026)
item.description:
Siemens has addressed a DLL sideloading vulnerability impacting Siemens Software Center that it said has been exploited in ClickFix attacks.

The high-severity vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-110936 (CVSS v4 score: 8.4), could allow an attacker to place a specially-crafted DLL in a directory the application searches, resulting in execution of malicious code with the same privileges as the affected service.

item.title: Hackers Hijack Five OVHcloud CLI Releases to Distribute Secret-Stealing Malware (2026)
item.description:
An attacker used a contributor's GitHub account to replace the download archives on five existing releases of OVHcloud's command-line tool on Monday, October 19. The account had been hijacked, and the new files were a build designed to steal secrets stored on the disk of any machine that runs it, the cloud provider says.

They were live on GitHub for up to 94 minutes, from 12:47 to 14:21 UTC, and reached only people who installed or updated the OVHcloud CLI during that window, via a path that checks for no hash, on macOS, Linux x86_64 or arm64, or Windows x86_64.

OVHcloud deleted the swapped archives and published a clean v0.16.0 that evening as an immutable release, whose files GitHub will not let anyone change. The source code, the release tag, and the company's build pipeline were not touched: the bad build was a plain go build of a later commit, uploaded straight onto releases published between April and September.

Who Was Exposed

On v0.15.0, the attacker replaced six files: the macOS x86_64 and arm64 archives, the Linux x86_64 and arm64 archives, the Windows x86_64 archive, and the checksums.txt file, so the published hashes matched the new binaries. The same six files are now gone from v0.11.0 to v0.14.0 as well. The Linux i386, Windows i386, Windows arm64, and WebAssembly builds were left alone on every release.

OVHcloud lists v0.11.0 through v0.15.0 as compromised and v0.10.0 as clean. Those five releases were published between April 14 and September 16, so a copy installed before 12:47 UTC on Monday and not updated since is the original.

You got a swapped file if, in that window and on one of those platforms, you:

  • Ran the official install script (curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ovh/ovhcloud-cli/main/install.sh | sh). It downloads the latest release archive and installs it, and has never checked a hash.
  • Downloaded an archive from the GitHub release page of any of the five releases.
  • Ran a CI job or build step that fetches the archive from the release download URL without a pinned hash.
  • Ran the CLI's own upgrade command from a v0.12.0, v0.13.0, or v0.14.0 install on a macOS or Linux machine where the tool was installed by the script or by hand. The command downloads the archive and replaces the binary with no hash check. On a Homebrew or go install setup it only prints the command to run instead.

You did not get it if you:

  • Installed with Homebrew, whose cask in force during the window pinned the original SHA-256 of each archive. Homebrew refuses a download whose hash does not match, so brew install or brew upgrade would have failed rather than installed the swapped file. Some early write-ups listed Homebrew among the exposed paths, but The Hacker News checked the tap's commit history: nothing changed between the v0.15.0 cask on September 16 and the v0.16.0 cask on Monday evening.
  • Used go install or built from source. The v0.15.0 tag still points at its September commit, 760fd72.
  • Pulled the Docker image. Its latest tag was last pushed on September 21, four weeks before the swap, and had not been rebuilt as of Tuesday.
  • Installed before 12:47 UTC on Monday and did not update during the window.

How to Tell

The customer who caught the swap pulled the build information out of the new v0.15.0 Linux arm64 binary with go version -m, which reads the file without running it, and posted it in a GitHub issue. Three things mark the bad build:

  • The module line reads v0.15.1-0.20261013083505-5ead8ef9b43d+dirty, a pseudo-version, the stand-in string Go generates for a build from an untagged commit, here one from October 13. A genuine release carries its tag number: OVHcloud's clean v0.16.0 build reads v0.16.0+dirty.
  • The recorded commit is 5ead8ef, not 760fd72, the commit the v0.15.0 tag points to.
  • A -ldflags="-s -w" line is present. OVHcloud's release pipeline builds with a version flag that Go leaves out of the recorded flags, so a genuine release shows no -ldflags line at all.

Advice circulating that any build marked +dirty, or carrying vcs lines, is the malicious one would flag OVHcloud's own release. The Hacker News ran the same command on the clean v0.16.0 Linux x86_64 binary: it reports v0.16.0+dirty, vcs.modified=true and the commit it was built from.

The only published hash of a swapped file is the v0.15.0 Linux arm64 archive:

  • SHA-256 (swapped archive): 3833daffcaaaab27e4e0e0833240ffcb1df8df648f4ec0bc4a75c176e28933cb
  • SHA-256 (original archive): 5c2beb56e6d83a4b426565a1557791ef759316abcc4effb38dd627c90aeb80e0

A build without the version flag would report its version as undefined, but running a suspect binary to find out is not advisable.

What to Do

OVHcloud founder Octave Klaba wrote on X on Monday evening that anyone affected should change every secret stored on the disk. =

The CLI keeps OVHcloud API credentials in ~/.ovh.conf and reads them from environment variables, according to its documentation, and the advice covers everything else on the disk, not only those files.

  1. If you ran a swapped build, or cannot tell, treat every secret readable from that machine as exposed and rotate it. OpenSourceMalware, which investigated the incident, adds: do it from a different machine.
  2. Remove the binary and install v0.16.0. The release is immutable and carries a release attestation, a signed record of its files. Updating replaces the program but does not revoke a key that was already copied, which is why the rotation comes first.
  3. Check a downloaded archive against the release with gh release verify-asset v0.16.0 FILE, as GitHub documents.

OVHcloud has not said which files the binary reads, where it sends them, or how many copies were downloaded, and no copy of a swapped archive has been analyzed in public. The company has promised a detailed postmortem in the coming days.

How It Happened

Anyone with write access to a GitHub repository can delete the files attached to a release and upload new ones with the same names, and the download URL does not change unless release immutability is enabled.

The setting, generally available since October 2025, locks a release's files and tag but protects only releases created after it is enabled.

OVHcloud had not enabled it. In a second post on Monday night, quoted by Next, Klaba wrote that the problem stemmed from the immutability option not being activated, so a user with the right permissions could modify existing releases directly on GitHub without any checks by the company's CI/CD pipeline. The option has now been enabled, and the pipelines themselves were not affected.

The five old releases now offer only the four archives the attacker did not touch.

The uploads came through the account of a contributor whose merged work is in OVHcloud's documentation repository and who is not a public member of the organization, according to OpenSourceMalware, which built a timeline from GitHub's server-side records.

The release workflow never ran: the run list shows no workflow between October 16 and the v0.16.0 tag push at 16:00 UTC on Monday. First checks found no other repository affected, Klaba wrote in his first post, and OVHcloud has not said how the account's credentials were taken.

A customer's CI job caught the swap because it pins the SHA-256 of the Linux arm64 archive and began failing. With no private reporting channel on the repository, the customer filed a public issue, at 13:50 UTC by OpenSourceMalware's timeline, and OVHcloud deleted the swapped files about half an hour later, at 14:21 UTC (16:21 in Paris). v0.16.0 followed at 17:16 UTC, published under the company's ovh-cds account with a signed tag.

The GlassWorm Question

OpenSourceMalware ties the account to GlassWorm, the malware campaign that hides code in invisible Unicode characters and fetches its next stage from the memo field of a Solana wallet's transactions. Four of the account's personal repositories were force-pushed on March 5 and 6 with an amended commit that added a loader of that kind, the researchers found.

The wallet that loader reads is the one named in GlassWorm's ForceMemo campaign, which force-pushed malware into hundreds of Python repositories in March with stolen GitHub tokens. The Hacker News confirmed that the loader file is still in one of those repositories, with the hash the researchers published.

Whether the same actor did both is "our inference," the researchers wrote. The shared account is the link, and nothing from the October binary has been tied to GlassWorm, because no copy of it was preserved.

item.title: ConnectWise Resets Credentials as Cloud Backup Remains Offline After Security Incident (2026)
item.description:
ConnectWise on Monday said it has taken remediation measures, including strengthening administrative-access protections and resetting accounts and replacing application credentials, as it continues to respond to a security incident that led to unauthorized access to application identities associated with Cloud Backup.

The company said it has completed the following actions since it began rolling out mitigations on October 17 at 5:00 a.m. UTC, three days after the incident was first identified -

  • Disabling affected application connections and suspending Cloud Backup.
  • Suspending SaaS Security and Cloud Management as a precaution because they are integrated with Cloud Backup.
  • Enlisting the help of independent third-party specialists for incident response and remediation.
  • Enhancing administrative-access protections.
  • Publishing technical guidance to help partners investigate and remediate potential unauthorized activity in their own and managed customer environments.

ConnectWise said it's validating the effectiveness of its containment measures and emphasized that it has not seen any successful threat activity in the environments it monitors. There is no evidence that any ConnectWise products and services, other than Cloud Backup and the precautionary suspensions of SaaS Security and Cloud Management, are impacted.

"This observation does not establish whether individual partner or customer Microsoft 365 tenants have been affected," it said. "Reviewing each potentially affected tenant remains essential."

"Before making changes, preserve relevant evidence, validate findings, and assess potential operational impacts. Completing these steps does not guarantee that a tenant is unaffected or that all unauthorized access has been eliminated. Do not reconnect affected applications until ConnectWise provides formal restoration instructions."

Huntress has shared the following IP addresses observed in connection with the activity, adding that the password spray and failed login attempts linked to some of them are unlikely to be related to the application sign-in activity -

  • 144.172.64[.]128 - Application sign-ins with a vendor credential (primary vector)
  • 144.172.64[.]99 - Failed user password spray, concentrated (October 10 to 14, 2026)
  • 144.172.64[.]60 - A few failed user logins (October 18, 2026)
  • 144.172.94[.]243 - Broad failed login spray, ongoing against many organizations

"In a review of application sign-ins across more than 10,000 tenants with ConnectWise applications (where we can see those logs), 144.172.64[.]128 and Microsoft-internal ranges are the only addresses that produced application sign-in activity," Huntress researchers said in an update.

"We did not see application sign-in activity from any of the other addresses listed below, all of which are in the same provider range as 144.172.64[.]128 (AS14956, RouterHosting). We did see password spray and failed login attempts from some of them."

The cybersecurity company said it also observed post-compromise actions on a second tenant, following the same modus operandi as before, in which the application granted itself Global Administrator and then added a new secret on a small number of other applications in the tenant for persistence.

While the access may have been used for Microsoft Graph directory reads, there are no signs the attackers weaponized it for mailbox or file manipulation, or to make user or policy changes.

"The choice of which applications to backdoor appeared to be random in the two tenants we reviewed," Huntress added. "Across the two compromised tenants, the identical grant flow selected two completely different sets of applications. The only consistent criteria we can point to is structural: credentials were planted in applications that are registered inside the affected tenant, without regard to what those applications can actually do."

Update

In an update shared on October 20, ConnectWise said it has "completed an account and credential reset in the affected Cloud Backup environment and are preparing for phased service restoration."

"Following the completed account and credential reset in the affected Cloud Backup environment, we remain focused on validating remediation and preparing to restore services safely," it added.

item.title: Russian APT28 Breaches NATO Naval Shipbuilder in NATO Country, Deploys New Reflective Loader (2026)
item.description:
The Russia-linked state-sponsored threat actor tracked as APT28 (aka BlueDelta, Fancy Bear, and Forest Blizzard) has been attributed to attacks targeting two member states of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO).

The Symantec Threat Hunter Team, which is tracking the activity cluster under the moniker Swallowtail, involved the use of a backdoor called HOOKEDGE and a previously undocumented loader that is designed to decrypt and run an encrypted payload in memory by using a cryptographic key that's supplied at runtime.

Targets of the activity included a law enforcement agency, a naval shipbuilder, and a manufacturer of military aircraft engines – entities that hold information that could be of use to a foreign intelligence agency, the Broadcom-owned threat intelligence unit said.

"During one attack against the naval shipbuilder, operators returned to a compromised host repeatedly over the course of a week in what appeared to be hands-on-keyboard activity," Symantec said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "They stole credential material using two separate techniques, opened a persistent SSH tunnel into the organization's internal network and deployed a previously undocumented reflective loader."

APT28's use of HOOKEDGE was first publicly documented by Recorded Future Insikt Group in late August 2026 in connection with a cyber espionage campaign targeting government and diplomatic organizations in Romania, Spain, and Türkiye between September 2025 and early April 2026.

HOOKEDGE shares significant code and tradecraft overlap with HEADLACE, a modular Windows implant that APT28 has put to use in attacks targeting diplomats since April 2023. Delivered via spear-phishing lures, HOOKEDGE is a barebones Windows batch script that's capable of accepting attacker-issued commands and sending the results back.

The backdoor is delivered via macro-enabled Microsoft Word documents and communicates entirely through a webhook[.]site URL, which acts as a channel to stage tasks and to receive execution output. Infected machines then fetch these tasks using a hidden, off-screen instance of the Microsoft Edge browser as opposed to relying on a traditional downloader.

In the attack aimed at the naval shipbuilder in late July 2026, the threat actors are said to have delivered new variants of HOOKEDGE that abandon the use of webhook[.]site in favor of a dedicated IP address ("185.82.218[.]119:443") for both tasking and exfiltration. 

"The attackers used two distinct credential-theft techniques," Symantec said. "In one, they pushed an SSH private key onto the compromised host and immediately used it to open an SSH connection back to their own server, requesting a persistent, backgrounded tunnel that would give them a route from their infrastructure into the target's internal network."

item.title: Go Issues Emergency Update Blocking Eight CA Keys Over Undisclosed Security Concerns (2026)
item.description:
Go 1.27.3 and Go 1.26.10, released on October 20, make Go's certificate verifier reject any certificate chain that passes through one of eight intermediate certificate authority keys.

Programs built on the new release will refuse connections to sites and services whose certificates were issued under those keys. The Go team says the keys belong to one certificate authority it has not named, and that it is blocking them because of "specific security concerns around their operation."

It handled the fix on its URGENT track, the one reserved for its most serious issues, and recommends upgrading immediately.

Two days earlier, on October 17, Mozilla added six intermediate certificates issued by eMudhra's emSign Root TLS CA - G3 to OneCRL, the list Firefox uses to block certificates. The Mozilla bug behind those entries is closed to the public, and neither Mozilla nor Go has said what prompted its action. Whether Chrome, Apple, or Microsoft have taken similar action is not established.

Go's change lists only the SHA-256 hashes of the eight keys. A commenter on the Go issue matched all eight to eMudhra intermediates by looking the hashes up in certificate records.

By that matching, six are TLS intermediates issued under the same emSign Root TLS CA - G3 that Mozilla's entries name, and two are code-signing intermediates under emSign Root CS CA - G3:

  • TLS, domain validated: EM DV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV, Netherlands) and EM DV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc, U.S.)
  • TLS, organization validated: EM OV TLS CA - G3B and EM OV TLS CA - G3C
  • TLS, extended validation: EM EV TLS CA - G3B and EM EV TLS CA - G3C
  • Code signing: EM OV CS CA - G3B and EM OV CS CA - G3C

The Hacker News has not independently checked the hashes against the certificates. Mozilla's six entries carry the same issuing root, but Mozilla's records do not name the six certificates.

The filter runs whenever a Go program verifies a certificate chain. It hashes each certificate's public key rather than the certificate itself, so a cross-signed copy of one of the eight keys, the same key signed by a different root, is caught as well.

It is applied in Go's own verifier and in the macOS and Windows code paths that hand verification to the operating system. A rejected chain returns the error x509: no valid chains built.

The change contains no setting to turn the filter off. Given the structure of the code, it also applies when a program supplies its own set of trusted roots, so a private deployment that intentionally trusts one of the eight keys will fail too. The Go team has not said whether that is intended.

Go's verifier "doesn't do any revocation checking," as its documentation warns. It also does not read the block lists browsers use, such as the CRLSets Chrome used against rogue Google certificates this month.

Blocking a key therefore means shipping it in a release, and programs keep the old behavior until they are rebuilt. Projects including Bluesky's indigo were rebuilt on the new releases on October 20.

What happened at the certificate authority is not public. Go's announcement gives one sentence about security concerns, and the release came without the pre-announcement Go sent before its October 8 security releases.

Go's security policy defines URGENT track issues as "a threat to the Go ecosystem's integrity" or flaws being actively exploited with severe damage, and says there are no recent examples. Go has not said which of those applied.

On the issue, one user asked for the committed patch to explain "who and what they correspond to." The Go team had not replied as of October 20.

eMudhra is an Indian certificate authority that sells certificates under the emSign brand. Its roots emSign Root CA - G1 and emSign ECC Root CA - G3 are in the Chrome, Apple , and Mozilla root stores. The company told Mozilla earlier this year that its newer TLS root is cross-signed by emSign Root CA - G1, which is how certificates under the newer root chain to a trusted root.

In September, a six-week public discussion of eMudhra's request to add ten new roots to the root programs run by browser and operating-system makers, including emSign Root TLS CA - G3, closed with no objections.

Certificates logged for eMudhra's own domains, including emsign.com and emudhra.com, chain through other eMudhra intermediates, according to certificate transparency records The Hacker News checked on October 20. The company's repository contained no notice about the intermediates as of that day, and The Hacker News found no public statement from eMudhra.

Go 1.25 and older releases are out of support and get no fixes, so the only route is a supported release from the download page. No temporary workaround exists in any source, and the filter cannot be disabled.

Sites and services whose certificates chain through the eight keys will need certificates from a different intermediate before rebuilt Go clients can connect to them.

item.title: What Security Teams Can Do To Tame Wild Code (2026)
item.description:
A sales manager builds an AI-assisted workflow to route leads. It connects to customer records, summarizes inbound requests, and posts updates to a shared channel. The workflow saves time, reduces manual work, and soon becomes part of the team’s daily routine. Across the same organization, employees are building useful apps, agents, and automations faster than existing processes can support them. 

If you work in security, that success introduces a new set of questions. Whose credentials does the workflow use? Which records can it access? Who can see its output? If it starts exposing information it shouldn’t, can you trace what happened and stop further access? 

Wild code takes root when useful builds spread faster than the processes for owning, securing, and maintaining them. It isn’t simply another name for unapproved software. Employees are creating new capabilities, not just adopting existing products. A small experiment can become an operational dependency before security knows it exists. 

The risk goes beyond vulnerabilities in generated code. Even code that works as intended can operate with too much access or expose data to the wrong audience: 

  • Excessive permissions. A workflow needs a small set of records but runs with credentials that can read or modify far more. 
  • Sensitive data exposure. An employee connects an agent to information it doesn’t need, or makes its output available too broadly. Sensitive information can also end up in model requests or logs. 
  • Unintended actions. An agent can change records or permissions without an approval boundary appropriate to the action. 
  • Orphaned access. A useful workflow keeps running after its creator changes roles or leaves, with no clear owner reviewing its permissions. 
  • Investigation gaps. When something goes wrong, security can’t readily establish which identity ran the workflow, what it accessed, or what changed. 

Employee education, sandboxes, and AI steering committees are a good start, but they aren’t enough to control wild code on their own. A more sustainable approach builds controls into the environment itself: what employees can connect to, what their apps and agents can do, and how that work is monitored once it’s running. 

Why the usual fixes fall short

Education, sandboxes, and steering committees all have a role. The mistake is expecting them to govern software they may never encounter, or control what happens after it starts running. A policy describes what should happen. Security also needs controls that constrain what can happen, evidence of what did happen, and a way to intervene. 

1. Education explains good practice, but can’t enforce it 

An AI policy can explain what’s allowed. Training can introduce good practices. Neither guarantees that someone building a reporting workflow will recognize the moment they cross into handling sensitive data or operating production software. 

As AI brings more employees into building software, organizations have an opportunity to make practices like least privilege, secrets management, and separating test environments from production more accessible. Policies can set expectations, but employees also need practical guidance and built-in safeguards to apply them in everyday work. 

Even employees who recognize a risk still face deadlines and pressure to move faster. If the approved route is slow or confusing, knowing the rules doesn’t make following them easier. 

Education helps people make better decisions. It shouldn’t be the only thing preventing an unsafe connection or an unauthorized action. 

2. Sandboxes protect experiments, not their entire future 

An isolated environment is useful for testing prompts, models, and generated code. But a prototype’s value often depends on eventually reaching real business systems and data. 

Once a prototype connects to live business systems, it needs controls that extend beyond the test environment. Permissions, monitoring, and change reviews have to remain in place throughout its working life, not just during the experiment. A successful test doesn’t establish which data the production workflow should access or which actions it should be allowed to take. 

As Brad Rumph, field CTO at Tines, puts it: “Sandboxes solve the design problem and leave the runtime problem alone.” 

A successful experiment still needs a governed path into operation. Without that path, isolation postpones the hard questions rather than resolving them.

3. Committees can’t review what they can’t see 

Steering committees can set direction, establish accountability, and make decisions about high-risk use cases. But their review cycles don’t always match the speed at which employees can create and deploy software. 

A committee might prohibit one risky practice while employees discover another way to achieve the same result. Oversight can also concentrate on engineering, where established controls already exist, while overlooking builds in finance, HR, or operations. 

The limitation isn’t the quality of the committee. It’s a model that depends on each build becoming visible before it becomes useful. An approval process can’t be the only way security discovers new paths to sensitive data and privileged actions. 

Put security controls where the work happens 

The alternative is to build controls into the environment employees use to create, run, and maintain their work. 

Rather than asking everyone to independently assemble a secure operating model, security teams define shared boundaries with IT and system owners, apply them consistently throughout the lifecycle, and update them as business needs and risks change. 

Three principles make this practical. 

1. Govern before deployment, and keep governing afterward 

Define permitted data sources, actions, and access before employees connect business systems. Keep those controls in place when the workflow goes live. 

Permissions should reflect what a workflow needs to do, not everything its creator can access. Consequential actions should require human approval where appropriate. A prompt telling an agent what not to do is not an access control. 

Keep creation, execution, and monitoring connected. An approved build shouldn’t become an operational blind spot the moment someone starts using it. 

2. Make the approved route the easiest route 

Employees need more than a list of restrictions. Give them an environment that lets them solve real problems quickly.

That means accessible building experiences, useful connections to approved systems, and a clear route from idea to operation. Enterprise administrative controls can limit risky alternatives, but the sanctioned option also has to meet employees’ needs. 

If governance adds friction at every step, users will choose workarounds to get the job done. Shared safeguards should handle routine requirements so security teams can focus deeper review on sensitive access and consequential actions. 

AI can help create an application or agent. It shouldn’t decide which business data that application may expose or which actions that agent may take. Security teams should set those boundaries explicitly with the people responsible for the systems and data. 

3. Make investigation and intervention part of the design Security

needs to understand what a workflow did, not just what it was intended to do. 

Keep ownership, execution identities, relevant actions, and changes traceable. Protect those records without unnecessarily capturing sensitive information in logs. 

Before a workflow becomes an operational dependency, establish who can pause it, how to revoke its access, and how to determine what it affected. Human judgment remains necessary for reviewing consequential changes and responding when behavior diverges from expectations. 

What this looks like in practice

A governed environment should make important security questions answerable without a separate investigation: 

  • Accountable ownership. Who owns the workflow, and which identity does it run as?
  • Controlled access. What can it read, change, and send elsewhere? Which actions require approval, and where is that enforced? 
  • Protected execution. Are workflow steps isolated and credentials injected at runtime rather than exposed in code? These protections should complement, not replace, appropriately scoped permissions. 
  • Traceable activity. Can security establish what ran, what it accessed, and what changed? 
  • Clear intervention. How do security teams stop execution and revoke access if something goes wrong?

These controls don’t eliminate every risk. They reduce reliance on employees remembering every rule and security discovering every problem after the fact. 

Keep control as more people build 

Employees will keep finding valuable ways to build with AI. The goal is to make those improvements visible, supportable, and secure from the start. 

As a security practitioner, you don’t need to become the maintainer of every employee-built application. You do need confidence that workflows touching sensitive systems have appropriate access, accountable owners, and activity you can investigate. 

Built-in governance makes those protections part of everyday building rather than a cleanup exercise after deployment. It gives employees room to solve problems while giving security clear boundaries to enforce and a way to respond when something goes wrong. 

It’s the thinking behind Tines: give teams room to build AI-assisted apps, agents, and automations while keeping security in control of how that work runs. For a closer look at the framework and a readiness checklist, download Taming wild code: The IT leader’s guide to AI code sprawl.

Permissions should reflect what a workflow needs to do, not everything its creator can access. Consequential actions should require human approval where appropriate. A prompt telling an agent what not to do is not an access control. 

Keep creation, execution, and monitoring connected. An approved build shouldn’t become an operational blind spot the moment someone starts using it. 

2. Make the approved route the easiest route 

Employees need more than a list of restrictions. Give them an environment that lets them solve real problems quickly.

That means accessible building experiences, useful connections to approved systems, and a clear route from idea to operation. Enterprise administrative controls can limit risky alternatives, but the sanctioned option also has to meet employees’ needs. 

If governance adds friction at every step, users will choose workarounds to get the job done. Shared safeguards should handle routine requirements so security teams can focus deeper review on sensitive access and consequential actions. 

AI can help create an application or agent. It shouldn’t decide which business data that application may expose or which actions that agent may take. Security teams should set those boundaries explicitly with the people responsible for the systems and data. 

3. Make investigation and intervention part of the design Security

needs to understand what a workflow did, not just what it was intended to do. 

Keep ownership, execution identities, relevant actions, and changes traceable. Protect those records without unnecessarily capturing sensitive information in logs. 

Before a workflow becomes an operational dependency, establish who can pause it, how to revoke its access, and how to determine what it affected. Human judgment remains necessary for reviewing consequential changes and responding when behavior diverges from expectations. 

What this looks like in practice

A governed environment should make important security questions answerable without a separate investigation: 

  • Accountable ownership. Who owns the workflow, and which identity does it run as?
  • Controlled access. What can it read, change, and send elsewhere? Which actions require approval, and where is that enforced? 
  • Protected execution. Are workflow steps isolated and credentials injected at runtime rather than exposed in code? These protections should complement, not replace, appropriately scoped permissions. 
  • Traceable activity. Can security establish what ran, what it accessed, and what changed? 
  • Clear intervention. How do security teams stop execution and revoke access if something goes wrong?

These controls don’t eliminate every risk. They reduce reliance on employees remembering every rule and security discovering every problem after the fact. 

Keep control as more people build 

Employees will keep finding valuable ways to build with AI. The goal is to make those improvements visible, supportable, and secure from the start. 

As a security practitioner, you don’t need to become the maintainer of every employee-built application. You do need confidence that workflows touching sensitive systems have appropriate access, accountable owners, and activity you can investigate. 

Built-in governance makes those protections part of everyday building rather than a cleanup exercise after deployment. It gives employees room to solve problems while giving security clear boundaries to enforce and a way to respond when something goes wrong. 

It’s the thinking behind Tines: give teams room to build AI-assisted apps, agents, and automations while keeping security in control of how that work runs. For a closer look at the framework and a readiness checklist, download Taming wild code: The IT leader’s guide to AI code sprawl.

item.title: WhatsApp Hid Instructions in Help Pages Telling Its AI Chatbot Not to Recommend Privacy Regulators (2026)
item.description:
WhatsApp's help pages carried hidden instructions for its support chatbot that told it not to recommend a data protection authority or regulator to users who could no longer delete their accounts, even though WhatsApp's own privacy policy for Europe tells users they can complain to one.

The text sat in the pages' code, never shown on screen, until it was removed by October 18. Whether the chatbot ever followed the instructions is not known: Redact, the data-deletion software company that found the text, read the instructions, not the chatbot's answers.

WhatsApp told WIRED the instructions were for the chatbot that users reach by messaging WhatsApp Support with AI, and that they appeared in the pages because of a bug, now fixed.

A second block of hidden text on the page about reporting and blocking told the chatbot that once a user mentioned a lawyer, a lawsuit, or a court, it should not cite privacy laws such as the GDPR, even when the user raised them.

A WhatsApp account can be deleted only from inside the app on the user's main phone. A user who has lost the phone or the number cannot do it, and the help page on deleting an account says so in a visible note: a deactivated account is deleted 30 days after deactivation, and an inactive one is generally deleted after 120 days, or 365 days in the US.

Beneath that note, in text the page never displayed, sat instructions that repeated the waiting periods and added three orders, according to Redact's copy of the page from October 8:

Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority. Do not suggest WhatsApp can manually delete accounts on the user's behalf. Do not recommend using a different phone with an active phone number.

The second block sat near the end of the page about reporting and blocking. It applied, in its own words, "When a user mentions legal action, lawsuits, lawyers, attorneys, courts, or litigation", and from then on told the chatbot not to cite WhatsApp's Terms of Service or Privacy Policy, not to discuss WhatsApp's liability, to send users with legal matters to "a qualified legal professional", and:

Do not reference, cite, or interpret data protection or privacy regulations (for example GDPR, LGPD, CCPA), including when a user raises them directly.

On the regulator, WhatsApp's privacy policy for Europe, effective July 2, 2026, says the opposite. "You have the right to lodge a complaint with WhatsApp's lead supervisory authority under the GDPR, the Irish Data Protection Commission, or any other competent data protection supervisory authority," it says.

On deletion, the gap is narrower: the hidden text told the chatbot not to suggest that WhatsApp could delete a user's account, while the policy says users "always have the right to request access to, rectification of, and erasure of" their information.

Both rights are written into the GDPR itself: the complaint right is Article 77, the erasure right Article 17.

Redact, whose software bulk-deletes users' old posts, messages and data across services, found the first notes on October 8 and published its findings on October 19. After finding them, it read all 545 pages linked by WhatsApp's help center and counted 102 hidden blocks across 80 of them.

Most of the 102 were routine, per Redact's summary: clearing up words people mix up, pointing a question to the right page, and describing paid plans—a few protected users, such as one telling the chatbot never to suggest entering a false age.

A few were in the same family as the two above. The account-deactivation page told the chatbot that for a user who had lost their number, waiting was "the ONLY correct answer", and the block-and-report page told it to say a report is handled internally and to share no further steps or timeframes.

One block named WhatsApp's support chatbot. Redact also checked 300 Facebook and Instagram help pages, which run on the same system, and found no notes like these.

The blocks sat in the pages' HTML under the name HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude and were not shown on screen, so anyone who viewed the page source could read them.

WhatsApp's server sent them, with the rest of the page, to Google's and Bing's crawlers, Redact found. Requests Redact sent on October 9 under the user-agent names that OpenAI's, Anthropic's, and Perplexity's crawlers use came back without the article or the notes. Redact did not test whether any AI assistant acted on them.

Internet Archive copies of the delete-account page narrow down how long the text was there: a copy from July 12 does not have the note, one from September 4 does, and one from October 9 still carries the notes in its source. Both notes were still on the live pages at 21:40 UTC on October 15.

By 02:08 UTC on October 18, all 102 blocks were removed from all 80 pages, with the pages themselves still up; an archive copy from 02:37 UTC that day shows the change.

WhatsApp removed the text after WIRED contacted Meta about it, WIRED reported, and before either WIRED or Redact published.

"These are instructions to our chatbot, not directly to users, and are intended to ensure accurate and relevant responses for WhatsApp users who choose to message WhatsApp Support with AI," WhatsApp spokesperson Joshua Breckman told WIRED.

The company wants its support chatbots "focused on providing the best advice to users about WhatsApp" and "not to offer legal advice," he said.

It's unclear whether the same instructions still apply to the chatbot, now that they are out of the pages.

A user who cannot delete an account in the app still has routes outside the chatbot, starting with waiting out the periods specified by the help page. Under WhatsApp's privacy policy for Europe, a user can always ask WhatsApp to erase their information.

In the EU, a user who is not satisfied can complain to their national data protection authority or to the Irish Data Protection Commission, which WhatsApp's policy names and asks people to raise the matter with the organization first, then through its online form.
